title: Cohen's Kappa Measures Something Else

body:
A statistic almost nobody computes by hand decides whether a benchmark reports a win. In the LLM-as-judge literature it is routine to see a judge "agree with humans 85% of the time" and, in the next sentence, "with Cohen's $\kappa = 0.42$". The two numbers are not describing different quantities on the same scale. They are describing different quantities, period. The gap between them is where most meta-evaluation lives, and the gap is where almost all the arguments about whether a judge is good enough actually sit — usually without anyone saying so.

The question worth taking seriously is not "which number is right". Both are right about something. The question is which thing each one measures and what each one asks you to assume. The chance-correction that produced $\kappa$ is a modeling choice, not a neutral floor; different corrections give different numbers on the same table, and the choice is almost never defended.

## Why this matters now

Three facts have collided. First, LLM-as-judge is now the default evaluation substrate for RAG, agents, preference optimisation, and open-ended generation. Second, serious reports have started treating a specific inter-annotator agreement number as the ceiling a judge must reach to be trusted — the NVIDIA "Judge's Verdict" study (Han et al., 2025) sets its Tier-1 bar at mean human–human Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.80$ computed on 1,994 items with three annotators each, and judges that do not clear that bar are excluded regardless of their raw percent agreement. Third, LLM-judge rubrics are often extreme in prevalence (safety labels where 2% of items are unsafe, factuality labels where 5% are wrong, hallucination labels in domain-specific pipelines) and the prevalence of the "interesting" class is exactly where $\kappa$ misbehaves most badly. The combination means the ceiling, the floor, and the comparison in between are all being read off a statistic whose paradoxes have been in print since 1990.

## The derivation, properly

Fix two raters $R_1, R_2$ labelling $n$ items into $C$ categories. Let $p_{ij}$ be the empirical proportion of items where $R_1 = i$ and $R_2 = j$, so $p_{i\cdot} = \sum_j p_{ij}$ is the marginal rate of category $i$ for $R_1$ and $p_{\cdot j}$ likewise for $R_2$. Observed agreement is $P_o = \sum_c p_{cc}$. Cohen's chance agreement is

$$P_e = \sum_c p_{c\cdot}\, p_{\cdot c},$$

and Cohen's kappa is the chance-corrected agreement

$$\kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}.$$

The denominator $1 - P_e$ is the headroom beyond chance that a perfect rater pair could attain; the numerator is how much of that headroom this pair used. Perfect agreement gives $\kappa = 1$; agreement at the chance level gives $0$; and $\kappa$ can go negative when raters agree less than independent raters with their marginals would.

What is $P_e$ actually? It is the agreement rate under a specific null model: each rater draws labels independently from their own observed category distribution, so cell $(i,j)$ occurs with probability $p_{i\cdot} p_{\cdot j}$. "Independently" and "their own distribution" are both choices. Scott's $\pi$ uses the *average* marginal $\bar p_c = (p_{c\cdot} + p_{\cdot c})/2$ and sets $P_e = \sum_c \bar p_c^2$, which assumes the raters share a distribution. Fleiss's $\kappa$ generalises Scott to more raters. Gwet's AC1 (below) picks a different null entirely. These are not refinements of a single quantity; they are different operationalisations of "what should chance mean here", and they can disagree substantially on the same confusion matrix.

## The prevalence paradox

Here is the simplest case where $\kappa$ breaks the intuition. One hundred items, binary rubric, both raters mark the positive class heavily:

|            | $R_2$ = A | $R_2$ = B |
|------------|-----------|-----------|
| $R_1$ = A  | 90        | 5         |
| $R_1$ = B  | 5         | 0         |

Raw agreement $P_o = 0.90$. Marginals: $p_{A\cdot} = p_{\cdot A} = 0.95$, $p_{B\cdot} = p_{\cdot B} = 0.05$. Chance agreement $P_e = 0.95^2 + 0.05^2 = 0.905$. Then $\kappa = (0.90 - 0.905)/(1 - 0.905) = -0.053$. Ninety percent of items agree, and $\kappa$ is negative. The reason is mechanical: when a category is overwhelmingly common, the chance expectation is almost everything agrees, so beating chance requires near-perfect agreement, and the two raters didn't.

The bias paradox is adjacent. Hold observed agreement fixed and swap marginals from matched to mismatched: $\kappa$ drops. Hold observed agreement fixed and *skew* the matched marginals: $\kappa$ drops again. Byrt, Bishop and Carlin (1993) show that $\kappa$ can be algebraically rewritten in terms of prevalence and bias indices and that this rewriting makes the dependence explicit; Feinstein and Cicchetti (1990) named the pair of paradoxes. Warrens (2010) gives a formal proof via the rearrangement inequality that for fixed $P_o$, $\kappa$ is maximised when marginals are balanced.

The practical consequence is that $\kappa$ is comparable *across* pairs of raters only when they face a similar prevalence of positive labels. In a safety benchmark where one dataset has 2% unsafe and another has 25% unsafe, the same judge can look much better on the second. This is a reporting problem, not a measurement problem — but the field often reports $\kappa$ alone.

## Rubrics are ordinal; unweighted kappa pretends they aren't

Most LLM-as-judge rubrics are not binary. A 1–5 Likert score has an ordering. Unweighted $\kappa$ treats "4 vs 5" and "1 vs 5" as equally wrong, which penalises a judge that is slightly off from humans more harshly than a judge that is off in different directions by the same amount. Cohen's (1968) weighted kappa fixes this with a weight matrix $w_{ij}$:

$$\kappa_w = \frac{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}\, p_{ij}}{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}\, p_{i\cdot}\, p_{\cdot j}}, \quad w_{ii} = 1,$$

so disagreements that are "closer" count for more. Standard choices are linear, $w_{ij} = 1 - |i-j|/(C-1)$, and quadratic, $w_{ij} = 1 - ((i-j)/(C-1))^2$. Quadratic weighted kappa is, under mild conditions on the marginals, asymptotically equal to the intraclass correlation coefficient on the ratings (Fleiss and Cohen, 1973). That is a double-edged inheritance: it makes QWK comparable to ICC, but it also means QWK is behaving like a correlation, which can be high even when a judge is systematically harsher than humans by one point everywhere.

Krippendorff's $\alpha$ generalises further. Let $D_o$ be the observed average pairwise distance and $D_e$ the expected distance under random reassignment of coder decisions; then $\alpha = 1 - D_o/D_e$. The distance function $\delta(i,j)$ is chosen for the measurement scale: nominal ($\mathbb{1}[i \neq j]$), ordinal (squared differences of cumulative marginal frequencies between categories), interval (squared differences), or ratio. $\alpha$ handles any number of coders, missing data, and arbitrary category sets, which is why it tends to appear in NLP annotation studies with many annotators. It is not paradox-free either; the choice of distance is a modeling commitment.

## Gwet's AC1: a different null

The alternative that most directly addresses prevalence is Gwet's AC1. Gwet (2008) argues the paradox arises not from $\kappa$'s numerator but from its chance-agreement model: the independent-marginals null is implausible precisely when prevalence is extreme, because much of the agreement there is not "chance" in any useful sense — it is both raters correctly recognising the obvious. AC1 defines chance agreement as $\pi_e = \frac{1}{C-1} \sum_c \bar p_c (1 - \bar p_c)$, where $\bar p_c$ is the average marginal rate of category $c$. For binary ratings this collapses to $\pi_e = 2 \bar p (1 - \bar p)$, which goes to zero as the positive rate goes to 0 or 1 — exactly where $\kappa$'s denominator shrinks fastest. AC1 then plugs into the same shell: $\mathrm{AC1} = (P_o - \pi_e)/(1 - \pi_e)$. AC1 is not literally paradox-free (Wongpakaran and co-authors, as well as later work, have found residual edge cases), but it is well-behaved on the specific tables that break $\kappa$.

## A concrete anchor

Take a judge and a human each labelling 1,000 responses as factual (positive) or not. Judge's positive rate 0.20, human's positive rate 0.18. Joint cells: 150 both-positive, 50 judge-positive-only, 30 human-positive-only, 770 both-negative. Observed $P_o = 0.92$. By Cohen: $P_e = 0.20 \cdot 0.18 + 0.80 \cdot 0.82 = 0.692$, $\kappa = 0.74$. By Gwet AC1: $\bar p = 0.19$, $\pi_e = 2(0.19)(0.81) = 0.308$, $\mathrm{AC1} = 0.88$. Raw 92%, Cohen 0.74, Gwet 0.88. Same table, three different answers, each defensible under its own null.

```python
import numpy as np

def cohens_kappa(cm):
    p = cm / cm.sum()
    po = np.trace(p)
    r, c = p.sum(axis=1), p.sum(axis=0)
    pe = (r * c).sum()
    return (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

def gwet_ac1(cm):
    p = cm / cm.sum()
    po = np.trace(p)
    pi = (p.sum(axis=1) + p.sum(axis=0)) / 2
    C = cm.shape[0]
    pe = (pi * (1 - pi)).sum() / (C - 1)
    return (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

def weighted_kappa(cm, weights="quadratic"):
    p = cm / cm.sum()
    C = cm.shape[0]
    idx = np.arange(C)
    diff = np.subtract.outer(idx, idx) / (C - 1)
    W = 1 - np.abs(diff) if weights == "linear" else 1 - diff**2
    r, c = p.sum(axis=1), p.sum(axis=0)
    return ((W * p).sum() - (W * np.outer(r, c)).sum()) \
           / (1 - (W * np.outer(r, c)).sum())
```

Running these three on the same confusion matrix is the smallest honest sanity check for a meta-evaluation. If the three answers disagree substantially, the headline number depends on a methodological choice the paper probably did not justify.

## What this implies in practice

Report at least three numbers for any judge: raw agreement, chance-corrected agreement, and the two marginal distributions. Without the marginals, neither of the first two is interpretable. Second, pick the chance correction to match the task's prevalence and the rubric's level of measurement: unweighted $\kappa$ for roughly balanced nominal classes, quadratic weighted $\kappa$ or $\alpha$ (ordinal) for Likert rubrics, AC1 or Krippendorff's $\alpha$ with the appropriate distance for extreme prevalence. Third, treat inter-human $\kappa$ as a ceiling on what a judge can be expected to achieve rather than a target to beat; a judge whose $\kappa$ exceeds the inter-human $\kappa$ is suspicious, not strong, because the only way to clear a ceiling that no human pair clears is to be matching an artifact that humans disagree about. Fourth, do not compare $\kappa$ across tasks with different prevalence without saying so; comparing a safety benchmark's $\kappa$ to a factuality benchmark's $\kappa$ smuggles in a prevalence difference that the number alone cannot reveal.

## Limits and open questions

No chance-corrected agreement statistic is universally best; each embeds a different null. Weighted $\kappa$ with quadratic weights behaves like a correlation and will reward a judge that is biased by a constant shift as long as the shift is consistent — fine for ranking, misleading for calibration. Gwet's AC1 trades sensitivity to prevalence for a weaker chance model and is unstable when $C$ is large relative to the number of items. Krippendorff's $\alpha$'s ordinal distance depends on cumulative marginal frequencies, which couples the metric to the sample; two studies with different label distributions compute $\alpha$ with different distance functions. Beyond the metric choice, there is a deeper problem: all of these quantities measure reliability, not validity. A judge and a panel of humans can agree perfectly and all be wrong in the same way, and no reliability statistic will catch that. The usual counter — ground-truthing against expert consensus or against downstream task outcomes — is domain work that the agreement number cannot substitute for. Finally, for multi-annotator LLM-judge pipelines where the "annotators" are stochastic samples from the same model, independence across raters is a fiction, which makes every $P_e$ or $D_e$ wrong by an unknown amount. Nothing in the toolbox addresses that; it has to be designed around.

## Further reading

- Cohen, J. (1960). *A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales.* Educational and Psychological Measurement 20(1):37–46. [doi:10.1177/001316446002000104](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104). The original definition; a short, clear paper worth reading before any of the critiques.
- Feinstein, A.R. and Cicchetti, D.V. (1990). *High agreement but low kappa: I. The problems of two paradoxes.* Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 43(6):543–549. [doi:10.1016/0895-4356(90)90158-L](https://doi.org/10.1016/0895-4356(90)90158-L). The paper that named the prevalence and bias paradoxes.
- Byrt, T., Bishop, J. and Carlin, J.B. (1993). *Bias, prevalence and kappa.* Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 46(5):423–429. [doi:10.1016/0895-4356(93)90018-V](https://doi.org/10.1016/0895-4356(93)90018-V). The algebraic rewrite of $\kappa$ in terms of prevalence and bias indices.
- Warrens, M.J. (2010). *A formal proof of a paradox associated with Cohen's kappa.* Journal of Classification 27(3):322–332. [https://research.rug.nl/en/publications/a-formal-proof-of-a-paradox-associated-with-cohens-kappa](https://research.rug.nl/en/publications/a-formal-proof-of-a-paradox-associated-with-cohens-kappa). The rearrangement-inequality proof.
- Gwet, K.L. (2008). *Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement.* British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 61(1):29–48. [https://agreestat.com/papers/bjmsp2008_interrater.pdf](https://agreestat.com/papers/bjmsp2008_interrater.pdf). The paper that proposes AC1 and justifies its chance-agreement model.
- Krippendorff, K. (2011). *Computing Krippendorff's Alpha-Reliability.* University of Pennsylvania ScholarlyCommons. [https://repository.upenn.edu/asc_papers/43/](https://repository.upenn.edu/asc_papers/43/). The canonical description of $\alpha$, including the ordinal and interval distance functions.
- Han, S. et al. (2025). *Judge's Verdict: A Comprehensive Analysis of LLM Judge Capability Through Human Agreement.* arXiv:2510.09738. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09738). The study that fixes a 0.80 human-human $\kappa$ as a tier threshold and screens 54 judges against it.
- Bedemariam, R. et al. (2025). *Potential and Perils of Large Language Models as Judges of Unstructured Textual Data.* arXiv:2501.08167. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.08167](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.08167). A direct comparison of Cohen's $\kappa$ and Krippendorff's $\alpha$ in an LLM-as-judge pipeline, with explicit thresholds for the ordinal case.
